rewritten_text:
Further chances to observe them were bound to arise. Before long, Anne had spent enough time with all four together to form an opinion, though she was too sensible to admit it at home, where she knew it would please neither husband nor wife. While she thought Louisa had a slight advantage, she could not help believing, so far as she dared trust her memory and experience, that Captain Wentworth loved neither sister. They were more taken with him, yet even their feelings were not love. It was a brief fever of admiration, though for some it might, and probably must, develop into love. Charles Hayter seemed conscious of being neglected, yet Henrietta sometimes appeared torn between the two men. Anne longed to explain to them all what they were doing and point out some of the unhappiness they were risking. She suspected no one of deception. It gave her the deepest satisfaction to believe that Captain Wentworth had no idea of the pain he was causing. There was no triumph in his manner, no petty triumph. He had probably never heard of Charles Hayter’s expectations, or given them a thought. His only fault was accepting the attentions—for accepting was the right word—of two young women at once.

After a brief struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to withdraw. Three days went by without a single visit from him to Uppercross, a most marked change. He had even declined a formal invitation to dinner. When Mr. Musgrove found him on that occasion with several large books open before him, he and Mrs. Musgrove became certain that something was wrong, and spoke solemnly of his studying himself to death. Mary hoped and believed that Henrietta had firmly rejected him, while her husband remained constantly sure that he would turn up tomorrow. Anne could only think Charles Hayter was acting wisely.

One morning around this time, Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth had gone shooting together. The sisters at the Cottage were quietly occupied with their needlework when the sisters from the main house appeared at their window.

It was a beautiful November day. The Miss Musgroves crossed the little grounds and stopped merely to announce that they intended to take a long walk, and therefore assumed Mary would not care to accompany them. Mary, immediately offended by the suggestion that she was not a good walker, replied, ‘Oh yes, I should very much like to come. I am extremely fond of a long walk.’ From the girls’ expressions, Anne felt certain this was precisely what they had hoped to avoid. Once again she marvelled at the obligation seemingly created by the family’s habits: everything had to be announced, and everything done together, however unwelcome or inconvenient the arrangement.

Well, three or four months passed, and by then it was deep into winter. I’d been going to school pretty regularly and could do a little spelling, reading, and writing. I could recite the multiplication table as far as six times seven is thirty-five, and I don’t suppose I’d ever get beyond that even if I lived forever. Anyway, I never had much use for mathematics.

At first I hated school, but after a while I learned to put up with it. Whenever I got especially tired of it, I skipped a day, and the beating I got afterward did me good and raised my spirits. So the longer I kept going, the easier it became. I was getting somewhat used to the widow’s ways, too, and they didn’t grate on me so much. Living indoors and sleeping in a bed usually made me feel pretty hemmed in, but before the weather turned cold I sometimes slipped out and slept in the woods. That gave me a break. I still preferred the old ways, but I was beginning to like the new ones a little, too. The widow said I was making slow but steady progress and doing very well. She said she had no reason to be ashamed of me.

One morning at breakfast I accidentally knocked over the salt dish. I grabbed for some salt as fast as I could, meaning to toss it over my left shoulder and ward off bad luck, but Miss Watson stopped me before I could. ‘Keep your hands away, Huckleberry,’ she said. ‘You’re always making such a mess!’ The widow spoke up for me, but I knew perfectly well that wouldn’t prevent the bad luck. After breakfast I set out feeling anxious and shaky, wondering where it would strike and what form it would take. There are ways of keeping certain kinds of bad luck away, but this wasn’t one of those kinds. So I didn’t try anything; I just trudged along unhappily, keeping my eyes open.

I went down into the front garden and climbed over the stile that lets you cross the high wooden fence. An inch of fresh snow covered the ground, and I noticed somebody’s footprints. They came up from the quarry, stopped around the stile for a while, and then continued along the outside of the garden fence. It was odd that whoever it was hadn’t come in after hanging around there. I couldn’t understand it. There was something very strange about the whole thing. I was about to follow the trail around, but first I bent down to examine the prints.

Almost a year had passed since my father returned, and the seasons had nearly completed their cycle. It was the end of May. Fresh green leaves covered the woods, and the fields smelled sweetly of newly cut grass. I hoped the warm, gentle air and the beauty of nature might soften his feelings, bringing him peace and affection before I tried to persuade him to confide in me.

I therefore chose one of those evenings to make my attempt. I asked him to walk with me and led him into a nearby beech wood. Its light shade protected us from the bright, slanting rays of the setting sun. After we had walked silently for a while, I sat down with him on a mossy mound. Strange as it seems, I can still see the place. Ivy twisted around many of the slender, smooth trunks. Its glossy, dark green leaves stood out against the white bark and the pale leaves of young beech shoots growing from the older trunks. Moss grew among the short grass. Dead leaves from the previous autumn partly covered the ground, blown here and there into small heaps. A few moss-covered stumps stood nearby. The breeze stirred the leaves gently, and through the green canopy we could glimpse the clear blue sky. As evening deepened, sunlight reddened the distant trunks. The wind dropped completely, and a few birds flew past us on their way to roost.

This was where we sat together. When you hear everything that happened, all the terrible things that wounded our souls even in that peaceful place, you will understand why I remember it. Without those strange passions, it might have been a paradise for us. I studied it then, hoping its stillness would calm me and give me both courage and the words to persuade him. I saw all these details and absently recorded them in my mind while trying to put my thoughts into a suitable order for what I meant to say. My heart beat quickly as I gathered the strength to speak. I was determined not to let him turn me away, yet I trembled at the thought of how my words might affect him. At last, with great hesitation, I began:

“My dearest father, you have been so kind to me, and when you first came back you showed me such affection—such overwhelming affection. I hope that, because of this, you will forgive me for daring to speak to you as I do. I speak with all a daughter’s tender love, but also with the openness of a friend and an equal.
